stem: A 24-year-old woman knows the exact day she conceived. Today is exactly 20 days after fertilization. She asks what her embryo looks like right now.
oneliner: 24F + exactly 20 days after fertilization → which developmental stage is present?
ask: Which description best fits the embryo at this stage?

options.A: Bilaminar disc with only epiblast and hypoblast
options.C: Closed neural tube with visible limb buds
options.D: Trilaminar disc with an open neural plate
options.E: Mature placenta with an embryo resistant to teratogens

whyNot.A: This is **week 2**; by day 20 gastrulation has produced a **third germ layer**
whyNot.B: This is the **first week**, before implantation; day 20 is long after the embryo has **implanted**
whyNot.C: The neural tube closes during **week 4** and limb buds appear then; at day 20 the neural plate is still **open**
whyNot.E: The placenta matures much later, and at day 20 the embryo is entering its **most vulnerable** period (weeks 3-8)

answer: Trilaminar embryo with notochord and open neural plate
why: By **day 20 (week 3)**, **gastrulation** has produced **ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm**; the **notochord induces the overlying ectoderm** to form the **neural plate**, and somites begin to form. The **neural tube is not yet closed** (closure of the ends occurs in week 4).

idea.rule: Week 3 = gastrulation and neurulation begins; week 4 = neural tube closes and limb buds appear.
also: Week 1: fertilization, cleavage, blastocyst
Week 2: bilaminar disc, implantation, hCG secreted
Week 3: trilaminar disc, notochord, neural plate
Weeks 3-8 are the period of greatest teratogen risk; neural tube defects arise from failed closure in week 4

stem: A newborn with a 46,XY karyotype has ambiguous genitalia and testes in the inguinal canals. The epididymis, vas deferens and seminal vesicles are present, and there is no uterus. Serum testosterone is normal and dihydrotestosterone is low. At puberty, the child virilizes.
oneliner: Newborn + 46,XY + ambiguous genitalia + inguinal testes + epididymis and vas present + no uterus + normal T, low DHT + virilizes at puberty → enzyme?
ask: Deficiency of which enzyme best explains these findings?

whyNot.A: **CAH**: virilizes a 46,XX fetus with a uterus and ovaries; a 46,XY infant would have normal male genitalia, and DHT stays normal
whyNot.C: 46,XY undervirilization with **low testosterone and hypertension**, but here testosterone is normal
whyNot.D: Blocks **testosterone to estradiol**; a 46,XY infant has normal genitalia, and a deficient fetus virilizes the mother
whyNot.E: **CAH with hypertension** from deoxycorticosterone excess; DHT is not low, and a 46,XY child is not ambiguous

why: Testosterone converts to **DHT** by 5-alpha-reductase. **Wolffian structures** (epididymis, vas, seminal vesicles) need only testosterone, so they form. **Urogenital sinus and external genitalia** need **DHT**, so they stay ambiguous until pubertal testosterone surges.

idea.rule: Testosterone builds the internal male tract; DHT builds the external male genitalia.
also: Finasteride blocks the same enzyme (BPH, male pattern baldness)
AIS: androgen receptor defect with high T and normal-to-high DHT
Mullerian structures absent because AMH is intact

stem: A 2-year-old boy with a normal penis and scrotum is having an inguinal hernia repaired. The surgeon finds a uterus and fallopian tubes in the hernia sac, and one testis is undescended. His karyotype is 46,XY, and his testosterone is normal.
oneliner: 2M + normal male genitalia + hernia repair finds uterus and tubes + 46,XY + normal testosterone → missing fetal hormone?
ask: Absence of which fetal hormone best explains these findings?

whyNot.A: Builds the **Wolffian ducts** and drives descent; his **testosterone is normal** and his penis and scrotum formed
whyNot.B: Builds the **penis and scrotum**, which are **normal** here
whyNot.C: Not needed for **Mullerian regression**; Mullerian structures regress through **AMH**, not through lack of estrogen
whyNot.E: Feeds back on **FSH**; it does not cause Mullerian duct regression

why: Fetal **Sertoli cells** secrete **AMH**, which makes the **paramesonephric ducts regress**. Without it, a normal 46,XY male keeps **uterus and tubes**. Leydig-cell testosterone is intact, so the penis and Wolffian derivatives are normal.

idea.rule: Male development needs two hormones: AMH removes the female tract and testosterone builds the male one.
also: Testis-determining factor (SRY) triggers both
Mullerian ducts normally form tubes, uterus and upper vagina
Undescended testis is a common association

stem: An 18-year-old woman has primary amenorrhea. Breast development and pubic hair are normal, and estradiol and ovarian size are normal. Examination shows a 1-cm blind vaginal dimple. Imaging shows no uterus or cervix.
oneliner: 18F + primary amenorrhea + normal breasts and pubic hair + normal estradiol + 1-cm blind vaginal dimple + no uterus → origin of the dimple?
ask: From which embryonic structure does the existing vaginal dimple derive?

whyNot.A: These form the **uterus, tubes and upper vagina**, which are **absent** here
whyNot.C: Regress in a female; in a male they form the **epididymis and vas**
whyNot.D: Becomes the **clitoris** (or the penis in a male), not the vagina
whyNot.E: Become the **labia minora** (or the ventral penis), not the vaginal canal

why: The **lower vagina** comes from the **urogenital sinus** (sinovaginal bulbs), while the **upper vagina, cervix, uterus and tubes** come from the Mullerian ducts. When the Mullerian ducts fail (**MRKH**), only the short sinus-derived pouch remains; **normal pubic hair** and ovaries separate this from AIS.

idea.rule: Upper two-thirds of the vagina = Mullerian; lower third = urogenital sinus.
also: Uterus, tubes, cervix and upper vagina: paramesonephric ducts
Vestibule, urethra, Bartholin and Skene glands: urogenital sinus
Ovaries: gonadal ridge (normal in MRKH)

stem: A 22-year-old woman at 20 weeks of gestation has sharp pain in the groin and labia when she stands up quickly. The pain follows a band that passes through the deep inguinal ring. Examination is otherwise normal, and fetal activity is normal.
oneliner: 22F + 20 wk pregnant + groin and labial pain on standing + band through deep inguinal ring → which ligament?
ask: Stretching of which structure most likely causes her pain?

whyNot.B: A peritoneal fold that does **not pass through the inguinal canal**
whyNot.C: Carries **ovarian vessels** over the pelvic brim; it does not run to the labia
whyNot.D: Runs **back to the sacrum**; it does not enter the inguinal canal
whyNot.E: Runs **sideways** from the cervix to the pelvic wall with the uterine vessels; it does **not enter the inguinal canal**

answer: Round ligament of the uterus (gubernaculum remnant)
why: The **round ligament** is the female remnant of the **gubernaculum**. It runs from the uterine horn through the **deep inguinal ring** and canal to the **labia majora**, so uterine growth in pregnancy stretches it.

idea.rule: The gubernaculum becomes the scrotal ligament in males and the round and ovarian ligaments in females.
also: Ovarian ligament: upper gubernaculum remnant, ovary to uterine horn
Male gubernaculum guides testicular descent and becomes the scrotal ligament
Canal of Nuck: patent processus vaginalis along the round ligament (female hernia or hydrocele)

stem: A 21-year-old man is undergoing radical orchiectomy for a testicular mass. The surgeon identifies the muscle layer of the cord that elevates the testis and mediates the cremasteric reflex. It lies deep to the external spermatic fascia and superficial to the internal spermatic fascia.
oneliner: 21M + radical orchiectomy + muscle of cord that elevates testis + between external and internal spermatic fascia → which abdominal wall layer?
ask: Which abdominal wall layer gives rise to this muscle?

whyNot.A: Gives the **external spermatic fascia**, the outermost layer, not the muscle
whyNot.B: Gives the **internal spermatic fascia**, the innermost layer, not the muscle
whyNot.C: Contributes **no layer** to the cord; its lowest fibers join the **conjoint tendon**
whyNot.D: Becomes the **tunica vaginalis**, which covers the testis directly

why: The testis pulls abdominal wall layers into the scrotum as it descends. **Internal oblique** forms the **cremaster muscle and fascia**; **external oblique** forms the external spermatic fascia and **transversalis fascia** forms the internal spermatic fascia.

idea.rule: Cord coverings from out to in: external oblique, internal oblique, transversalis fascia.
also: External spermatic fascia: external oblique
Cremaster: internal oblique
Internal spermatic fascia: transversalis fascia
Tunica vaginalis: processus vaginalis (peritoneum)
